extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers learning to use unreliable narrators
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for creating and using an unreliable narrator in fiction (especially first-person), including types of unreliability, when and how to reveal it, and craft tips to make the device effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable narrator — definition / credibility compromised
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreliable narrator is one that is not to be fully believed. His or her credibility is compromised due to some admission of insanity or an obviously false claim that the reader knows is incorrect, or due to the story revealing information about the narrator that makes the reader question the believability of claims made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for dramatic effect to create an ending with a twist or to make the reader question if the narrator should be trusted. Examples cited: Poe's 'Tell-Tale Heart', Flynn's 'Gone Girl'.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person POV limitations as source of unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Any story told from first person point of view has limitations because recollection is subjective and might not include all relevant details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for omission include missed details, forgetting over time, self-preservation, avoiding negative consequences, or simply not noticing. Use these realistic limits to justify a narrator's unreliability and make it plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Pícaro (exaggerating/tall-tale narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who is prone to exaggeration and bragging and is unreliable due to his or her tendency for tall tales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Moll Flanders, Simplicius Simplicissimus, Felix Krull. Use boastful voice and exaggeration as the chief mechanism of unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Madman (mental-disorder-based unreliability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who has a mental disorder resulting in dissociation, schizophrenia or paranoia, making their narration untrustworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fight Club (insomniac narrator/Tyler Durden), Kafka's narrators, Notes on a Scandal, Pale Fire, American Psycho. Show symptoms or narrative contradictions that reveal dissociation or instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Clown (toying with truth and expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who toys with the truth and the reader's expectations, deliberately playing with veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tristram Shandy. Use playful, self-aware narration that signals manipulation of the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Naïf (limited understanding POV)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator with a limited understanding or point of view whose lack of comprehension makes their account unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rebecca (as a type), Huckleberry Finn, Holden Caulfield, Jack in 'Room'. Use limited knowledge, youth, or inexperience to justify misinterpretation or gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Liar (purposeful deception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who purposefully lies to the audience and manipulates the story through intentional falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: John Dowell in 'The Good Soldier'. Build deliberate inconsistencies and rationalizations that can later be unveiled as lies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed / multi-faceted unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Some unreliable narrators mix several categories (e.g., exaggeration + mental instability + deliberate lying).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alex in 'A Clockwork Orange' combines traits (antihero, admitted deception, drug use, fictional jargon). Be aware that combining types can create richer, layered unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator who evades truth out of self-preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who alters or omits facts to protect themselves from trauma or consequences, making their narrated version suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pi Patel in 'Life of Pi' gives a fantastical animal story that rescuers ultimately accept as a less traumatic alternate. Use plausible motives (trauma, shame) to justify alternative accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator who doesn't know all the truth (memory/awareness gaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose account is unreliable because they genuinely lack memory or awareness of events (e.g., due to blackouts, intoxication, or trauma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rachel in 'The Girl on the Train' — alcohol-induced blackouts make her explanations unreliable. Signal memory gaps, lost time, or cognitive impairment as the source of uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose / effect of using an unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an unreliable narrator can create a twist ending, psychologically thrill readers, and prevent anything being taken at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unreliability to hook audiences, create memorable characters, and structure revelations. Consider whether you want the device for suspense, character study, or thematic ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the narrator seem very clever (crafting believable deception)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the narrator lies on purpose, making him or her incredibly clever and intelligent helps sustain the deception within the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale from real-world lying: liars must cover bases and anticipate discovery. Show planning, foresight, and awareness of how lies could be exposed to make deception plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an out-of-character action to signal unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Having your narrator suddenly do something 'out of character' immediately calls their reliability into question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a surprising action or behavior early or at a strategic moment to prompt readers to reassess the narrator's trustworthiness — especially effective if you don't reveal unreliability immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider making the narrator the 'bad guy' but keep them likable
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the unreliable narrator a villain can make for compelling storytelling, but the narrator must retain redeeming qualities to keep readers engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'A Clockwork Orange', 'American Psycho'. Balance villainy with charm, humor, or insight so the reader continues to turn pages despite moral repulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the narrator authentic and believable
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a narrator is narcissistic, pathological, or mentally unstable, they should remain authentic and consistent within a believable framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict predictable patterns and realistic symptoms (if using a mental illness). Authenticity keeps readers engaged and prevents the device from feeling contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of revelation — don't reveal too much too soon
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid revealing the narrator's unreliability too early; readers assume truth and enjoy the surprise when their assumptions are overturned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pace the disclosure of contradictions or revelations. Let the narrator's voice carry trust initially, then slowly introduce evidence that undermines that trust to maximize dramatic effect.
